finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto the authenticated user object and persists it, so any user can set privileged or internal fields (e.g. role, isAdmin, id, email verification status, tenant/org id) and escalate privileges or take over other records.
finding.source: req.body of PUT /me (any authenticated user, attacker-controlled JSON)
finding.sink: req.store.save(req.user) persisting arbitrary attacker-chosen fields on the user record

trace.note: PUT /me handler; req.user assumed populated by upstream auth middleware
Object.assign(req.user, req.body) merges all body keys with no allowlist

finding.guards_checked: No field allowlist, schema validation, or role check in this file; only one file exists in the directory so no upstream middleware or store-side filtering is visible. Contrast with /me/profile (line 11), which correctly destructures only displayName and bio.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation, and users.js:6 persists it, so any authenticated user can set arbitrary fields. Only users.js is in the directory, so any upstream auth middleware or store-side filtering can't be seen. The safer /me/profile route at users.js:11 shows the intended pattern.

verdict_facts.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist, schema check or role check, then users.js:6 saves it, so any authenticated user can set arbitrary fields. The safe /me/profile route at users.js:11-12 shows the allowlist this route lacks.
